question: How do depth, per-block hidden width, embedding dimension, and residual scaling jointly determine whether a randomly initialized deep ResNet converges to a feature-learning mean ODE or a lazy limit?

key_findings.claim: At fixed embedding dimension and arbitrary hidden width, the finite ResNet's forward/backward training dynamics converge with depth to a neural mean ODE, with output error of order 1/L plus alpha divided by sqrt(LM).
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 1 couples the trained parameters to a stochastic mean-ODE process for a fixed number of gradient steps. The error decomposes into Euler depth discretization O(1/L) and Monte-Carlo sampling O(alpha/sqrt(LM)), so the product LM acts as an effective width.

key_findings.claim: The limiting dynamics are genuinely feature learning for order-one residual scale alpha, whereas alpha diverging yields a linearly parameterized lazy mean-ODE regime.
key_findings.evidence: The model's velocity field remains nonlinear in the trained measure at alpha=Theta(1). Section 3 rescales around large alpha and Theorem 2 gives convergence to a lazy ODE in which the learned map is linear in the limiting parameters.

key_findings.claim: For two-layer-perceptron residual blocks, complete feature learning across growing embedding dimension requires residual scale Theta(sqrt(D)/(LM)), and the bound becomes O(1/L + sqrt(D)/sqrt(LM)).
key_findings.evidence: The dimensional phase diagram analyzes forward signal, backward signal, and update sizes under parameterized initialization. Theorem 3 states the dimension-dependent coupling, implying LM must dominate D for the finite model to closely track its mean-ODE limit.

key_findings.claim: Synthetic experiments support the claimed exponent dependence on L, M, and D over the tested range, but do not validate optimization quality or task performance of the limiting regimes.
key_findings.evidence: Figures 2 and 4 measure deviations between sampled networks and constructed mean-ODE quantities and report slopes consistent with the upper bounds. Experiments use controlled teacher-style settings and a fixed small number of gradient steps rather than standard ResNet training on a benchmark.

key_findings.claim: Calling LM the hidden width is useful for the approximation theorem but should not be read as a universal capacity law: constants depend on fixed D, the horizon is finitely many gradient steps, and the theorem assumes smooth bounded blocks and tightly coupled initialization.
key_findings.evidence: Assumptions A and B impose regularity and boundedness; the main constants are dimension dependent before Section 4. The theorem controls a coupling to a particular mean process, not generalization, convergence to a minimizer, or long-time stochastic training.

method.core_idea: View a depth-L, width-M residual network as a joint Euler and Monte-Carlo discretization of a continuously deep neural mean ODE, then propagate the coupling through a finite number of gradient updates.
method.mechanism: Random units within each block approximate an expectation over a parameter distribution, while layers discretize depth. Propagation of chaos maintains approximate independence during training. Separate scaling analysis for two-layer blocks tracks activations, gradients, and updates as embedding dimension grows.
assumptions: Residual blocks and derivatives satisfy uniform smoothness and boundedness conditions.
Initialization is random, exchangeable, and coupled to the limiting process.
The number of gradient steps is fixed while depth/width limits are taken.

techniques.role: Controls dependence created by shared training updates.
Separates depth and hidden-unit approximation errors.
Classifies feature-learning and lazy residual parameterizations.

evaluations.setting: Synthetic ResNets varying depth L and block width M
evaluations.result: Log-log behavior was reported as tight in the 1/L and 1/sqrt(LM) dependencies.

evaluations.setting: Two-layer-block ResNets varying embedding dimension D
evaluations.result: Experiments supported the sqrt(D)/sqrt(LM) sampling dependence over the tested grid.
evaluations.baseline: Alternative residual scales corresponding to degenerate or lazy regimes

limitations: Guarantees cover a fixed finite training horizon, not convergence of practical long runs.
Smoothness/boundedness conditions exclude common nonsmooth blocks without approximation arguments.
No standard vision or language benchmark tests whether the recommended scaling improves learned representations.
The D-dependent result is specialized to two-layer perceptron blocks.
failure_modes: If LM does not dominate D, finite-network fluctuations need not vanish in the claimed feature-learning scaling.
Large alpha drives a lazy linearized limit rather than complete feature learning.
Other residual scalings can cause vanishing or exploding forward, backward, or update signals.
reusable_insights: Depth and within-block width can substitute statistically through their product even though their discretization errors differ.
Scaling laws should jointly preserve forward signal, backward signal, and parameter-update magnitude.
A finite-network-to-limit theorem is stronger when its empirical validation measures the coupling error rather than only end-task loss.
open_questions: Does the LM effective-width law survive stochastic minibatches, normalization, attention, and long training horizons?
Can dimension-uniform constants be proved for realistic Transformer blocks?
Which scaling best predicts representation change and downstream generalization rather than mean-limit proximity?

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Ordinary Differential Equations
competitive_landscape.difference: Neural ODEs take a deterministic continuous-depth limit; this paper adds random within-layer particles, feature-learning training dynamics, and a finite L,M error rate.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Global Convergence of Gradient Descent for multi-layer ResNets in the mean-field regime
competitive_landscape.difference: Ding et al. focus on global convergence of a mean-field PDE under overparameterization; the present work derives tight finite depth-width coupling rates and a feature/lazy phase diagram.

competitive_landscape.title: Tensor Programs V: Tuning Large Neural Networks via Zero-Shot Hyperparameter Transfer
competitive_landscape.difference: Maximal-update parameterization preserves update scales and hyperparameter transfer at large width; this paper instead couples depth and hidden width through a stochastic mean ODE and derives explicit residual scales.

competitive_landscape.title: Mean-field theory of two-layers neural networks: dimension-free bounds and kernel limit
competitive_landscape.difference: The two-layer analysis controls width particles without the simultaneous residual-depth discretization and embedding-dimension phase diagram developed here.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper gives tight depth-width error bounds for trained deep ResNets and identifies the unique two-layer-block scaling that retains complete feature learning as embedding dimension grows.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Three theorems couple finite models to feature and lazy mean-ODE limits, with synthetic exponent checks.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The joint Euler/Monte-Carlo view and LM effective-width rate sharpen separate depth or width limits. Its practical scope remains uncertain because the controlled finite-step theorem is several assumptions away from modern normalized stochastic training.
